newsitem.title: USA: Ad executives say tobacco industry targets youths.
newsitem.headline: Ad executives say tobacco industry targets youths.

text.p: More than half of some 300 advertising executives surveyed believe that a goal of tobacco advertising is marketing to teenagers despite cigarette companies' denials, according to a study released Wednesday.

The survey, sponsored by the Initiative on Tobacco Marketing to Children, a group of advertising, marketing and public relations executives, also found that the majority of advertising agency executives approve of some restrictions on tobacco advertising.

The findings reflect a split in the industry as a group of advertising organisations has sued the Food and Drug Administration to stop its proposal to regulate cigarette advertising. The groups argue that the restrictions violate their freedom of speech rights.

The tobacco industry, which has filed the key suit challenging the FDA's proposal, has until next Monday to file final briefs in the litigation pending in federal court in Greensboro, N.C. Arguments are scheduled for February.

David Milenthal, chairman of the Columbus, Ohio-based advertising firm HMS partners and a leader of the Initiative, said the survey results showed that advertising executives are concerned that advertising influences children to smoke.

"Members of our industry have spoken loud and clear. Not only do they feel strongly that advertising influences kids to start smoking, but they want changes to reduce the effect these ads have on the most vulnerable segment of society," he said.

The survey, which was conducted by the New York advertising agency of Shepardson, Stern & Kaminsky, states that while the tobacco industry says the goal of advertising is only to influence adult smokers to switch brands, "the majority of advertising executives interviewed believe that the industry also intends to market cigarettes to teenagers, both those who already smoke and those who are non-smokers"

That view, according to the survey, is particularly strong among the most senior segment of executives. The study said that 77 percent of those with more than 20 years of experience say that marketing to teenage smokers is a "goal" of tobacco advertising.
The majority of those surveyed said they felt that advertising does increase smoking among minors and that it makes smoking more appealing and socially acceptable.
The study found that most participants were generally supportive of most of the proposed FDA regulations.

Of those, 84 percent agreed that outdoor advertising should be banned near schools and playgrounds and 62 percent agreed that tobacco companies should not distribute t-shirts, hats and other items that kids may wear.

When asked if they supported a prohibiton on brand name sponsorship of sporting and entertainment events, 55 percent agreed and 42 percent disagreed. Fifty-four percent agreed to limiting ads in magazines with significant youth readership and 44 percent disagreed.

While the overwhelming majority of advertising executives interviewed support voluntary guidelines on tobacco advertising to minimise the impact on children and teens, relatively few said they believed those guidelines would be followed or enforced.
